A southpaw is a left-handed person — someone whose dominant hand is their left hand. That's the foundation of the word. Everything else builds from there.

The word is informal and conversational, not clinical or technical. It sounds sporty and vivid. Calling someone a southpaw carries no negative meaning — if anything, it often sounds cool or slightly admiring, the way you'd point out something that makes a person stand out.

Outside any specific sport, "southpaw" is simply a colorful synonym for a left-handed person:

  • "She's a southpaw — she writes, draws, and throws all with her left hand."
  • "I didn't realize he was a southpaw until he reached for the pen."

You can use it to describe anyone in daily life. The word just paints the picture more interestingly than saying "left-handed."
In sports — where the word truly lives

The word is used most often in sports, where being left-handed changes how you play and forces opponents to adapt. Here's how it works in each major context:

Baseball

In baseball, "southpaw" almost exclusively refers to a left-handed pitcher — the player who throws the ball toward the batter.

Left-handed pitchers are genuinely less common than right-handed ones, which makes them valuable. Their pitches break and curve in directions that feel unfamiliar to right-handed batters (who make up the majority of hitters). A left-handed pitcher's curveball, for example, curves away from a right-handed batter in a way that's harder to read than a typical right-handed pitcher's ball.

  • "The team brought in their southpaw to face the lineup of right-handed hitters."
  • "Great southpaws are rare and highly sought-after in professional baseball."

This is probably the single most common sports-specific use of the word.

Boxing

In boxing, "southpaw" is used with slightly more precision. It refers to a boxer who fights from a left-handed stance — and understanding that stance is key.

Here's how boxing stances work:

A typical right-handed boxer (called an orthodox fighter) stands with their left foot and left hand forward — that forward hand is used to jab and probe. Their right hand is held back, because that's their stronger hand, and it's saved for the big, powerful punch (the cross or the hook).

A southpaw does the exact opposite: right foot and right hand forward, with the left hand held back as the dominant power punch. When a southpaw throws their left hand, it's coming from an unexpected angle — a wide, looping path that most fighters haven't trained against.

This is why southpaw boxers are considered tricky opponents. The vast majority of fighters train by sparring with orthodox fighters. When they suddenly face a southpaw, the angles are reversed, the punches come from the "wrong" side, and everything feels unfamiliar. Many coaches specifically seek out southpaw sparring partners just to give their fighters practice.

  • "Nobody in the gym wanted to spar with him — he was a southpaw with a knockout left hook."
  • "The champion struggled against the southpaw's unusual angles and kept getting caught by the left hand."

Famous southpaw boxers include Manny Pacquiao, Marvin Hagler, and Joe Frazier — all known for aggressive, left-hand-dominant fighting styles.

Other sports

The word appears across other sports too — cricket (a left-handed batsman or bowler), tennis (a left-handed player), golf (a left-handed golfer), and even fencing or martial arts. The meaning is always the same: the person uses their left side as their dominant, leading side.

  • "The left-handed tennis player is a southpaw — his serve spins in the opposite direction from most players."

These two phrases mean the same thing, but they feel different. "Left-handed" is neutral and factual — the kind of thing you'd write on a medical form. "Southpaw" is vivid, informal, and conversational — the kind of thing a coach, commentator, or friend says.

You'd say: "The doctor noted he was left-handed" — not "The doctor noted he was a southpaw."

But you'd say: "The commentator called him a natural southpaw with deadly accuracy" — not "The commentator called him left-handed."

In boxing, it's worth knowing that "southpaw" technically describes a fighting stance, not just inborn handedness. A right-handed person could choose to fight from a southpaw stance (some do this deliberately to confuse opponents — it's called being an "unorthodox" or "converted" southpaw). So in boxing, the word describes how you fight, which usually — but not always — lines up with your natural dominant hand.

Outside boxing, southpaw always just means a left-handed person, full stop.

• Everyday use: A left-handed person. Full stop.
  • Baseball: A left-handed pitcher specifically.
  • Boxing: A fighter who leads with the right foot and right hand, holds the left hand back as the power punch — the left-handed fighting stance.
  • Register: Informal, conversational, slightly sporty or admiring in tone.
  • Core thread through all uses: Left-handedness — either as a physical trait or as the basis of a fighting stance.
